headline: OpenAI Codex /goal feature finishes 85% of scoped tasks with persistent, self-checking loops
summary: The /goal feature, generally available since May 2026, enables Codex to loop until a task is complete, using self-evaluation and budget tracking. This persistent approach significantly boosts its success rate on defined coding challenges.
details: OpenAI's Codex /goal feature is reporting an 85% to 90% success rate on well-scoped maintenance work in internal testing. This capability, shipped in Codex CLI 0.128.0, became generally available across CLI, IDE extension, and the Codex app in version 0.133.0 on May 21, 2026.

Unlike a standard stateless Codex turn, the /goal feature allows you to set a specific objective. Codex then continuously loops, checking if the goal is complete, with the only hard stops being a 'done' evaluation or an exhausted token budget.

This persistent behavior is achieved by automatically injecting two prompts at the end of every turn: `goals/continuation.md` to check completion and decide whether to continue, and `goals/budget_limit.md` to track token consumption. The loop proceeds until one of these conditions is met.

A key improvement in version 0.133.0 introduced dedicated storage for goals, making them persistent across active turns and even CLI restarts. Previously, goals were session-scoped and would terminate if the CLI process died.

The loop pattern employed by OpenAI is known as the "Ralph loop," where an agent self-checks its output to determine continuation. Codex enhances this by adding budget accounting and a persistence layer, with prompt injection handled automatically.

For successful goal completion, the task must have a binary success check, a tight scope, and an observable success condition from within the session. Examples include fixing failing tests or type checks, which return a clear pass/fail result.

Failure modes primarily fall into two categories: scope creep and unprovable completion. Scope creep occurs when fixing one issue inadvertently creates another, which the agent, given its narrow goal, doesn't recognize or address.

Unprovable completion happens when the agent cannot self-check its work, such as with subjective tasks like "refactor this service to be more readable." The agent will make changes and stop, but cannot verify if the code is objectively "better."

Architectural changes also frequently fail, as they involve ambiguous decisions like module boundaries or service responsibilities. The 85% success rate likely applies to a curated set of maintenance tasks with clear success criteria, not open-ended design work.

headline: AI phishing kits rent for $88/week, enabling industrial-scale scam texts
summary: Google's lawsuit against Outsider Enterprise reveals AI-powered phishing tools are rented for just $88 a week, drastically lowering the barrier for large-scale scam operations. This has enabled 2.5 million texts in two weeks, scamming hundreds of thousands.
details: An AI-powered phishing kit, reportedly used by the Chinese cybercrime operation Outsider Enterprise, rents for just $88 a week. This low cost has enabled the group to send 2.5 million scam text messages in two weeks, defrauding hundreds of thousands of victims.

For years, running large-scale phishing required significant effort in building convincing fake sites and writing non-obvious copy. Google's complaint states that Outsider Enterprise sold all of this as a subscription product, leveraging AI to streamline the process.

The same generative AI tools used to ship products faster are also lowering the cost of faking those products. Google accuses Outsider Enterprise of using Gemini to build fake pages and hosting some on Google Drive and Google Cloud.

AI didn't invent phishing, but it removed the two main limiting factors: the cost of writing convincing content and the skill needed to build fake sites at scale. This allows for industrial-scale operations where a low hit rate still yields significant returns.

The asymmetry is stark: sending millions of messages costs almost nothing, making even a 0.1% success rate profitable. This explains the continued growth of smishing (SMS phishing) globally, with sophisticated fake messages appearing in inboxes worldwide.

For consumers, the key defense is to stop judging legitimacy by how polished a message looks, as AI ensures perfection. Instead, focus on how you arrived at the link, trusting only paths you control like opening an app directly or typing a domain.

This case is also a warning for developers and service providers: any service with a login is now a template. Outsider Enterprise allegedly shipped over 290 ready-made clones of legitimate brands, making it trivial to add more.

The broader lesson for anyone building with generative AI is that the same models drafting marketing pages can create perfect clones of others. "It looks professional" is no longer proof of legitimacy; provenance and better trust signals are critically needed.
